📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.
  • Recent findings suggest that the commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook.
  • Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.

Recent findings suggest that the commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement, Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world.

Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading.

According to recent reports, "We're also getting interest from latest entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added.

After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities.

"We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig mentioned.

"Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he remarked.

Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not presently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes.

But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration.

"I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said.

It has been revealed that crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory.

"I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig stated, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable.

When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig remarked, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate.".

"I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he noted.

It has been revealed that selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets.

Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps.

According to recent reports, "We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling.".

— CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

Floods Force Gaza to Choose Between Clean Water and Pumping Out Sewage

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.
  • “The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” states municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.
  • Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.

“The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” states municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.

Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters. In some tents in Al Maghazi, the water was well over a foot deep, Jawad notes.

It has been revealed that for Hanan Saied, 46, the storm soaked the bedding and clothing she shares with her seven children. She lives in a shelter in Al Maghazi with mud walls, cracks, and plastic sheeting covering the roof, which WIRED Middle East visited.

Recent findings suggest that “The house flooded, and stones and mud fell on us,” Saied says. “The bedding was soaked, and the children’s clothes were soaked.”.

It has been revealed that her children used buckets to move water away while her eldest son tried to repair the shelter. Saied spent the night holding her daughter, Sara, who she indicates has asthma, trying to keep her warm.

Gaza’s Government Media Office has said at least 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians had flooded within 12 hours.

On 8 November, the Israel account on X, run by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, posted, “Contrary to popular belief, Israel does not control the weather.” The post did not explicitly mention Gaza floods.

It has been revealed that the flooding comes after widespread destruction of Gaza’s housing. An April assessment by the European Union, United Nations, and World Bank found that more than 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed and around 1.9 million people internally displaced, often repeatedly.

It has been revealed that by 8 November, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that 1.4 million people—65 percent of Gaza’s population—were living in tents or shelters. Humanitarian partners had received appeals from more than 26,000 households whose shelters or belongings had been damaged.

In Al Maghazi, Jawad describes five displacement sites across the camp’s western and northern areas. Parts sit on low ground where rainwater accumulates without an outlet.

His teams used pumps to move water outside the displacement sites. But the problems extend beneath the streets.

Sources indicate that israeli bombardment has damaged sewage manhole covers in Al Maghazi, Jawad says. Other covers have been stolen or deteriorated over time. The resulting openings allow rainwater to pour into sewage networks unable to accommodate the extra volume, causing wastewater to overflow.

“The sewage networks become unable to accommodate the quantities of sewage in addition to the rainwater that leaks into the manholes because the covers are missing,” he says.

Replacement covers are unavailable locally, while materials needed to fabricate alternatives are scarce and expensive. The municipality cannot afford all the work required. Keeping the water supply running takes priority.

“I consider spending money on maintaining wells or maintaining generators to operate water wells a higher priority than allocating some of that money to maintaining sewage manhole covers,” Jawad claims.

It has been revealed that these shortages extend across Gaza. In its November 5 report, OCHA remarked Israeli authorities continued to impose particularly tight restrictions on engine oil, lubricants, spare parts, and new generators. Systems for pumping floodwater and sewage were already failing.

Restoring more sustainable power supplies, the agency added, depended on Israeli permission to import solar panels, reconnect the electricity grid, and restart Gaza’s power plant.

The Israel Defense Forces did not respond to WIRED Middle East’s request for comment on restrictions affecting the entry of equipment and supplies needed for flood prevention and infrastructure repairs.

Jawad claims trucks and earth-moving machinery are needed to bring material to displacement sites where water collects on muddy ground, improving conditions beneath and around tents.

The consequences also reach clinics. Dr Asma Saleh, a general practitioner at the Al Maghazi clinic of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), reports an increase in children presenting with respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses as the rainy season begins.

Saleh states the clinic sees around 120 children daily, including approximately 22 with influenza-like illness diagnosed from symptoms and 13 with gastroenteritis.

“The inhumane living conditions, collapse of infrastructure, the flowing streets contaminated with sewage, and the shortage of medical supplies are all factors that profoundly impact the health care system in Gaza,” she says.

For Saied, the immediate concern is getting Sara through the next storm. Her daughter has more frequent asthma attacks during winter, she indicates, and the family has neither a nebuliser nor electricity to operate one.

“My older son spent hours repairing our worn shelter using simple tools, but I don’t know what to do during upcoming storms.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI on Friday unveiled ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.

The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.

OpenAI mentioned its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.

"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

Industry observers note that chatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts.

Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company noted it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.

It has been revealed that openAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout" feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for consumers to find and compare products.

Nayak stated ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.

"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.

OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active people and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb stated OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.

"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.

It has been revealed that merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines stated Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.

According to recent reports, openAI stated Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.

Industry observers note that "It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak mentioned. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants.".

#209. Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (967 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle.
  • To swiftly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways.
  • It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

To swiftly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an matter of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

In a recent development, it starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Owners also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

One of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

According to recent reports, continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Recent findings suggest that another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google noted that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes.

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google claims it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:.

According to recent reports, for the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has officially entered the "Hey Gemini" era with the launch of its first Android XR smart glasses yesterday.

In a recent development, google has slowly been integrating Gemini into pretty much every aspect of its apps and services. You can now find Gemini everywhere, from the best Android phones to Google services like Sheets, Gmail, and pretty much everything in between.

And with the company retiring Google Assistant last year, Google has been gradually switching everything over to Gemini. The launch of its first Android XR "Intelligent Eyewear" smart glasses yesterday is yet another example of that shift.

When Google unveiled its Android XR-powered smart glasses yesterday, the tech giant revealed that users will be able to access Gemini not by saying "Hey Google," as we presently do on Android phones and smart home devices, but by using the new "Hey Gemini" hotword instead.

Saying "Hey Gemini" on these smart glasses will trigger the same Gemini-powered AI assistant we've been using for quite some time now. However, this is the first time Google has introduced a different hotword for Gemini, moving away from the familiar "Hey Google" phrase and signaling a clear shift in how the tech giant wants people to interact with its AI assistant.

According to recent reports, for now, the "Hey Gemini" hotword doesn't work on other devices like Android phones or smart home devices, which still rely on "Hey Google" to activate the assistant. However, it's pretty clear that Google is moving toward making Gemini the face of its AI-powered experiences, and the fresh hotword could eventually make its way to other devices as well.

Sources indicate that of course, Google hasn't confirmed whether or when it prepares to replace "Hey Google" across its other products. But with "Hey Gemini" now making its debut on Android XR smart glasses, it'll be interesting to see how long the familiar Google Assistant hotword sticks around.

Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has ties to the chipmaker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.
  • It has been revealed that "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J.
  • Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.

The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.

It has been revealed that "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.

Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.

The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11.

By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.

According to recent reports, even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.

Recent findings suggest that those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing newly introduced export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.

An ethics expert noted the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, remarked that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great.".

"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.

There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.

"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.

Industry observers note that cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.

As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.

According to recent reports, trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.

But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.".

Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes.".

Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy. At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing.

That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing, as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China.

Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026, with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.

Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.

"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.

The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.

Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30, the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.

Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.

In a recent development, most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured, a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.

As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to the Nov. 11 Axios report, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show.

On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN declared a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.

Industry observers note that "That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the manufacturer's quarterly earnings call that day.

Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The Upcoming York Times reported Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.

In a recent development, howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, according to the Nov. 10 Axios report.

On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN unveiled the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs.

On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.

Sources indicate that it is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.

In a recent development, by the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.

IREN was not the only manufacturer in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.

In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.

Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor, also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.

It has been revealed that ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium, which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.

It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.

Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.

In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick confirmed the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false.".

Recent findings suggest that TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.

Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from Howard Lutnick's push to expand AI data centers.

Industry observers note that and on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons, D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.

The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled.".

"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons remarked Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

AdultFriendFinder, on the other hand, is a DM-sliding free-for-all. In fact, the concept of connecting with strangers is kind of the point. In that respect, AFF operates like a regular dating site (it's one of the OGs in that field, dating back to 1996), whereas FetLife is more of a social media website for building local kink communities.

AdultFriendFinder isn't totally without these resources, but they're not as user-friendly or as accessible to total newcomers to the world of kink.

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.

Latest Update: My 9 Favorite Pickleball Paddles From 3 Years of Testing (2026)

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The sport of pickleball—a cross between tennis and badminton, played with a hard plastic ball—is 60 years old, having been invented near Seattle in 1965.
  • Pickleball has exploded in popularity, and with that newfound popularity comes an arms race with paddle makers in a quest to make the best pickleball paddles.
  • Updated November 2026: We've added a new paddle from Paddletek and a couple of accessories, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sport of pickleball—a cross between tennis and badminton, played with a hard plastic ball—is 60 years old, having been invented near Seattle in 1965. For most of that time, paddles were made of laminated wood and were mostly found in gym classes and retirement communities.

Pickleball has exploded in popularity, and with that newfound popularity comes an arms race with paddle makers in a quest to make the best pickleball paddles. Paddle technology is improving, too. This is my third year testing the latest crop of pickleball paddles, and they've made another leap forward. Among my long-standing favorite paddles like the Selkirk Vanguard Control Invikta, there are two latest ones—including the Diadem Warrior BluCore—that step back from the raw power of heat-molded plastic cores by substituting foam cores that offer a very consistent and controlled feel. Here are my most up-to-date paddle picks for every style and level of play.

Updated November 2026: We've added a new paddle from Paddletek and a couple of accessories, and updated links and prices.

Selkirk is a wildly popular paddle maker, but I was not a huge fan of the higher-end paddles in the lineup after testing dozens of models over a few seasons.

It has been revealed that the Selkirk Vanguard Control Invikta sold me on the brand. It’s still the best all-around paddle for most people and the one I'd recommend to anyone who doesn't demand the ability to hit huge overhead smashes—the Invikta is not thermoformed and doesn't have quite the same power as paddles that are. (Thermoformed paddles are molded with heat and injected with foam, while traditional paddles are made by stacking up layers like a sandwich.).

Industry observers note that what the Invikta offers, however, is exceptional control and consistency. This paddle is shockingly well balanced and feels great in the hand, thanks to Selkirk's upgraded octagonal grip. Every time you swing the Invikta, the hit feels like you expect it to feel, and the ball goes exactly where you expect it to go. It's especially nice to have confidence in that consistency while developing more spin (I was a practitioner of the now-banned spin toss serve and I'm still in rebuilding mode), because you don't have to worry about a goofy bounce from a dead spot caused by a botched thermoforming process. The Invikta does offer impressive spin, thanks to a T700 raw carbon face and a larger-than-average sweet spot.

According to recent reports, I was not sure what to expect from Diadem's fresh BluCore paddle, which is among a handful of new paddles that have replaced the standard honeycomb polymer core with closed-cell foam—they sent me a sample of the stuff, and it looks like you could make a gas station cooler out of it. That foam is substantially more durable—it has a lifetime warranty, in fact—over the long haul and is also not at risk of delaminating in extreme temperatures if, for example, you leave the paddle in the car on a scorching summer day while you grab patio margs.

Given how far this paddle is outside the norm, and the fact that it's priced at the upper end of the range, I wanted to put real time in before recommending it. What I found was that the BluCore took some time to get used to, but it's now the paddle I play with the most. The foam core makes for a softer and more forgiving feel—it's like the suspension on an old Cadillac coupe. While I don't feel like I'm getting the most out of my serve, I especially love this paddle in defensive situations against better players. It plays consistently from edge to edge and has a nice, big sweet spot.

Whether foam ends up dominating the pickleball market remains to be seen, but people who play nearly every day will also appreciate that this paddle uses an aramid carbon fiber face that is more durable than raw carbon and that the foam absorbs more vibration.

★ Another foam core paddle: I was also pretty impressed with the Selkirk Labs 008, a latest foam core paddle from the maker of our top pick for most people above. The 008 has a more traditional feel and a smaller but more poppy sweet spot. Because this paddle uses a T700 raw carbon fiber instead of more durable aramid carbon fiber, I fear the face will lose its effectiveness even when the core remains solid.

If you've never played pickleball, this is a good place to start, so you can get a feel for the game without sinking too much dough. For less than $30, you get two paddles and a few balls.

Sources indicate that ★ A beginner upgrade: The SLK Evo Power XL 2.0 is the paddle I bought myself from a substantial-box sporting goods store after a few times playing with the cheap set off Amazon. I bought this paddle based on its excellent feel and still love swinging it. Selkirk bills this paddle, which has a fiberglass face that provides limited spin, as an ideal pick for beginners and pickleball-curious tennis players.

It has been revealed that this is the fourth edition of the signature paddle made for pro pickleballer Ben Johns, the reigning number one singles player in the world. I've tested the previous two Johns' paddles along with a half-dozen others from Mayland-based Joola—including a few now-banned paddles that were the subject of a brief calamity last year.

Recent findings suggest that the current Persus paddle, which is fully approved for tournament play, has a ton of pop. This paddle is thermoformed, meaning it's heat-pressed together and virtually indestructible. It’s a little heavy on the head and has less power than the previous generation, but with better control. The sweet spot is also a little larger but less sweet. Whack one right on the money, though, and the ball jolts off it.

★ Budget mashing: If you want to mash balls, but on a budget, go for the Phantom Eternal. A carbon-fiber face for $60 is a great bargain, and the Phantom Eternal is overall a very solid paddle. I didn't find it all that precise compared to competitors that are more than double the price (there are dead spots at the top of my paddle, around the eyes). However, I loved the thick, slightly sticky grip and appreciated the unique graphics. Mostly, though, I found myself swinging for the fences with this paddle—something about it makes you feel like you can smoke a return right next to your opponent's foot.

According to recent reports, full disclosure: I have never really understood the appeal of an open-throat pickleball paddle. Having a gap between the handle and paddle face that mimics a tennis racket does not provide any obvious benefit—those who have examined the claimed benefits have seemingly concluded they don't exist.

It has been revealed that however, some people like the look and feel of these paddles, so I have tested a handful and found this paddle from Onix to be the best of the bunch. It's also my pick if you want an edgeless paddle (another design quirk I don't favor). This paddle is fun to swing hard and has a very consistent face, though the two rubber inserts designed to lessen vibration aren't doing much for me, as this paddle plays very bumpy.

It has been revealed that diadem's Hush is a thermoformed paddle that employs a foam-covered face to eliminate the controversial pop sound (which I love). Diadem claims it's the quietest paddle in the world; I found the noise level more akin to tennis than pickleball.

According to recent reports, the best compliment I can give the Hush is that it handles mostly like any other paddle. This is a very welcome surprise given that its face feels like a pool noodle. The paddle only weighs 8 ounces but seems heavier. While the dense, spongy surface doesn't offer as much pop as a standard thermoformed paddle, it's got as much as the standard layer-build paddles on this list. I still haven't found any obvious dead spots, though it is understandably a little mushy. Diadem claims the foam is also helpful for spin, but in my testing I wasn't able to generate much. This paddle is not tournament-approved, but if you're looking to play at odd hours or practice against a wall at your house, it could save you a lot of drama.

Pickleballs are cousins to Wiffle balls. If you grew up playing backyard baseball, you probably remember that the holes in the plastic balls allowed them to spin in unpredictable ways when thrown or hit correctly. The same is true of pickleball, where a skilled player with the right paddle can cause problems for an opponent. A serve with spin is so much harder to return that the official rules of the game now ban players from swirling the ball during a drop serve.

I have not mastered topspin and backspin but the Reload has me working on the technique. The biggest problem with amateurs creating topspin is that the gritty paddles that deliver it are either technically illegal or rapidly lose effectiveness. This gets annoyingly technical very quickly, but rule 2.E.2.a of USA Pickleball's Equipment Standards manual lays out a standard and protocol for max grittiness and establishes that “a coefficient of friction test based on protocol (IAW) ASTM D1894-14 is used to measure the general friction characteristics.” Carbon fiber is the best material for getting up to the threshold but not over it, but the carbon surfaces wear down like a pencil, meaning paddles lose grittiness over time—a normal paddle loses half its grit within a month of play according to a study done by Reload's owner (who obviously has a competing product to sell). This phenomenon is well known in pickleball circles, and pro players often switch out their paddles after every game or tournament to have fresh grit.

Reload paddles offer an innovative solution by making the carbon-fiber surface replaceable. The Reload paddle itself is a very neutral and balanced middle-weight thermoformed paddle with the standard polypropylene core. The magic is in the peel-and-stick carbon fiber sheets for the hitting surface, which give you fresh grit for $50 instead of dropping another $200 and sending a months-old plastic paddle to the landfill. I found the replacement process refreshingly forgiving, as my first attempt was misaligned on one side, but I couldn't tell which side got a second stick.

In a recent development, recess pickleball paddles are known for their unmatched style—these are the prettiest paddles in the game. They come in a wide variety of colorful patterns and have great grips with plenty of cushioning made from faux leather. They also come with an embroidered canvas cover.

It has been revealed that with a gritted fiberglass surface over the standard polymer honeycomb core, they do not offer the same performance as the high-end carbon-fiber pickleball paddles. Recess paddles do seem to have a smaller sweet spot than some other brands. However, when you play a shot well, this paddle is excellent. I’ll take the satisfaction of a well-played ball hit with a stylish Recess paddle over almost anything on this list.

Because I'm always testing new paddles, I usually roll up to the courts with about $2,000 worth of high-end paddles in my Babolat bag. My 10-year-old daughter can pick any paddle she wants, and the one she likes best is this $43 paddle from Pickle Genius. At 13 millimeters, it's a little thinner than most paddles here, which means she can swing faster and harder. It has a very neutral feel, mid-grade pop, and simple design.

Here are some other paddles we've really liked in testing, including some older models still on sale still worth considering.

Paddletek Honeyfoam ESQ 16 mm for $100: The day I first began testing this paddle, it stopped my singles partner dead in her tracks. “What is that?” “Paddletek Honeyfoam.” “Don’t they all have honeycomb?” “No, honey-FOAM.” Three foam types do make for a larger sweet spot as promised, and the softer surface makes for a slower ball and increased control. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar liked the classic “pop” sound, and so do I, so it’s a little sad to hear it muffled here, but I’ll take the softer thwack if it means I can catch the ball a little off-center and still put it where I want it. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that joola's Tyson McGuffin Magnus 3 for $248: This previous pick is still available used. Joola not only has the top-ranked player in the world but also number six, Tyson McGuffin. What I love about the McGuffin signature paddle is the sound. You may know that the sound of a pickleball game is quite controversial. I happen to like the sound (I do not live next to a pickleball court), and I like the sound of this paddle best of all. The hot-pink McGuffin paddle is one of the hottest on the market right now and frequently out of stock. It's a banger, using “Propulsion Core technology” that offers serious power, and I find myself too often hitting long with it. However, that sound. Pawwwwp. It's so satisfying. Pawwwwp. It sounds like a well-hit baseball by your favorite team to walk off in the bottom of the ninth.

Bagsmart Advantage 15L Paddle Tote for $21: I’ve been carrying this sturdy bag for almost a full season now, and it somehow looks just as pristine as the day I got it. Though the styling is quite loud (people sometimes think it’s a 4th of July or America-themed bag), it’s comfortable to carry with two sets of handles: short and over-the-shoulder. It’s also got a thick, rubbery bottom so you can put it right on the ground even when the court is wet. There’s also a luggage pass-through and plenty of room for a laptop, change of clothes, and multiple paddles. (Plus a water bottle holder.) —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that sqairz XRZ2 Pickleball Shoes for $159: Though best known for golf shoes, Sqairz as a brand is known for its square toe box, which allows for toes to naturally splay out during play. My favorite part is that the laces have rubbery little nubs on them to keep them from coming untied. The fit seems small at first, but they stretch out fast—maybe even too much, as I have narrow feet and I’m starting to feel like there’s too much movement in them. I'd consider going a half-size down. That said, I do appreciate the sole's stability, even if they're a bit heavy. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that I’m not an expert player (I'm somewhere between a 4.0 and a 4.5 on the USAP's Player Skill Rating), but I’ve now tested more than 100 paddles on indoor and outdoor courts over the past three years. At one point I played in a weekly pickleball league, though I don't anymore. I also test the paddles against a Slinger pickleball machine which is very helpful, as the machine consistently fires balls with a lot of spin and power. After playing with piles of paddles—and having players of various skill levels try them and share their thoughts—I feel confident that this guide has a paddle recommendation for you, whether you're a beginner or a pro pickleball player.

Pickleball paddles are restricted by a size formula similar to the one airlines use: The paddle can’t be longer than 17 inches and the combined length and width of the paddle cannot exceed 24 inches. A standard paddle is 16 inches long and 8 inches wide, but some elongated paddles use the full 17 inches and tend to have more power than wider options. There is no restriction on the thickness of the paddle; thin paddles can be about one-third of an inch thick, while thick paddles can be up to three-quarters of an inch thick.

It has been revealed that you'll see me using this term a few times in this guide. “Pop” is the pickleball parlance for how aggressively the ball bounces off the paddle face—you can think of it as an analogue to how "bouncy" a basketball is.

It has been revealed that the latest buzzword in pickleball circles is “dwell time,” which means how long the ball stays in contact with the face of the paddle before bouncing back off. Because your body is providing torque when you swing, the longer the balls sits—time measured in nanoseconds—on the face of the paddle the more spin will be created and the harder your shot will be to return. It gets very nerdy very rapidly. I would love to speak about the dwell time of the paddles I've tested, but my personal sense of the number of nanoseconds the ball is in contact with the paddle is not appropriately fine-tuned.

How Much Do Pickleball Paddles Weigh?

Recent findings suggest that there is no rule about a pickleball paddle's weight, but almost every paddle hovers around 8 ounces. I went out of my way to test the biggest range of paddles I could find and ended up testing paddles that were within about an ounce of each other. Light paddles tend to be about 7.5 ounces, whereas heavyweight paddles are about 8.5 ounces. More important is the distribution of that weight—paddles that offer more power tend to be top-heavy. I prefer paddles with a balanced feel.

Are All Pickleball Paddles the Same Shape?

According to recent reports, pickleball paddles tend to look fairly similar shapewise. In my testing, I tried several outliers, including a Joola paddle with a rounded shape more like a tennis racket, and several Selkirk paddles with a cutout between the paddle face and handle designed to minimize air resistance. I think the standard shape is still best.

What Are Pickleball Paddles Made Of?

Old-fashioned wooden paddles still exist, but inexpensive fiberglass paddles are how I started playing. You can nab a beginner set for $30 (see “Best for Beginners”), and it could be six months before you feel the need to upgrade. That mentioned, the paddles recommended here tend to have a carbon-fiber face, which is stiff and light, offering lots of pop. I also tested some graphite paddles, which are cheaper, heavier, and softer than carbon fiber. If your budget doesn’t allow you to start with carbon fiber, I’d recommend starting with cheap fiberglass and then jumping to carbon fiber. Note that when I mention materials, I mean what's used for the face of the paddle—nearly all paddles have a similar honeycomb-shaped polymer core. Pricier paddles tend to cut that core in a way that creates even gaps on the edge and use heat-pressing to seal the face to the core.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, 9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

According to recent reports, apple published a latest security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Recent findings suggest that today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from people than a wake word.

Recent findings suggest that person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Recent findings suggest that much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”.

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this latest exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this latest level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

Overall, this new technical post reads like Apple laying the privacy groundwork for the always-listening, always-watching products that are here and coming in the near future. It’s the privacy-first approach we’ve come to love from Apple and further demonstrates its lead on this front. I highly recommend checking it out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Google Health app update was supposed to bring a slew of performance improvements for some of the best fitness trackers, but instead, it unleashed a bug that's been plaguing Fitbit people for the past few days.

According to the slew of reports on Reddit, a number of basic health metrics have gone missing from the view in the mobile app on both Android and iOS, including overnight vitals such as resting heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and HRV. Google rolled out its 5.12 patch last week, which appears to be the common link between user reports online.

The bug isn't limited to just one device either — owners on the latest Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge models, the Fitbit Charge 6, and Fitbit Sense 2 are all experiencing this absence. These vitals are tracked daily to establish patterns and highlight changes in your health, so if they miss a day or two, it could have a huge impact on your readings.

But despite these health metrics vanishing from thin air, it doesn't necessarily mean that your device has stopped tracking your data altogether. In some user cases, the device has continued monitoring health patterns, but the app has just failed to display them.

Still, it's not ideal, and users have been quick to jump on Google's case — but the company has issued some reassurance that it's looking into it.

Among the wave of reports on Reddit, one user went the extra mile and reached out to Google directly, sharing the email they received in response: 'it's a joke' they shared.

Other people turned to Google's support forum for answers, where one of Google's product experts mentioned they had escalated the issue.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

However, the issues in the app are persisting, and Google has yet to find a solution, leaving people to find their own workarounds for the time being.

One method you can try is simply logging out of the Google Health app and logging back in again. Some consumers have found this helpful, but it hasn't been the golden ticket for others. In that case, try uninstalling the Google Health app altogether and redownloading it, which is a bit of a pain, but it's worth a shot.

We've reached out to Google for comment on the status of the problem.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a fresh bar for secure payments by agents.”.

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI notes ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to consumers’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”.

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro customers,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”.

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

According to recent reports, before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The tech giant emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

#193. No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2326 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the upcoming air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote.
  • Newly introduced systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway.
  • None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the upcoming air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly unveiled that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”.

Newly introduced systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.

None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.

It has been revealed that according to Joby Aviation, the firm that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?

Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this newly introduced technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” states a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”.

Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.

According to recent reports, in 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.

Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April.

With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, significant players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious intends for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.

Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the firm unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.

According to recent reports, for more than a decade, various eVTOL builders have been promising that production models were just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very notable, safe, careful dance,” notes Greg Bowles, Chief Policy Officer at Joby Aviation.

Sources indicate that silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” says Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.

AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.

That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.

It has been revealed that the ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology manufacturer DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”.

It has been revealed that joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within Upcoming York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The manufacturer has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.

These demo flights, Bowles notes, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.

To start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers. Ultimately, for the eVTOL concept to be viable economically, all such aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.

Sources indicate that given the scale of the challenge, the entry point of AI into human passenger flight won’t be as flashy as piloting eVTOLs; it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling.

In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data firm Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford mentioned in a press release.

Joby Aviation’s S4 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft.

The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” claims the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”.

In a recent development, some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”.

Then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”.

Some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an vital improvement,” Schiavo states. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”.

Recent findings suggest that michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he indicates. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”.

In a recent development, that sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”.

The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he notes, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”.

It has been revealed that with two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.
