Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead battery might do more damage than you think.
  • If your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger.
  • It has been revealed that granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead battery might do more damage than you think.

If your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger. One minute you're cranking away on some crucial spreadsheet for work, and the next, you're staring at your own face reflected in a black screen. Aside from the jump scare of the latter, there could actually be a bigger risk to letting your laptop battery completely drain.

It has been revealed that granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery. Some of it hinges on the type of battery and how you use it. No matter how you cut it, though, a total drain isn't ideal, even if it won't set off a disaster if it happens from time to time. Nevertheless, here's what happens when you fully drain your laptop battery.

Industry observers note that on the whole, lithium-ion batteries, like those you'd find in a laptop, are pretty low maintenance and have several perks, such as being able to charge fairly quickly. In a perfect world, you wouldn't get all the way down to 0%. HP explains that if you want to extend your laptop battery's life as long as possible, it's best to keep the charge somewhere between 20% and 80%. Others might recommend charging to 40% to 80%. Either way, this also takes a bite out of the myth that you should drain your battery before recharging it in the name of longevity.

Repeatedly letting your battery drop to low levels can cause wear to the battery. Staying within a safe range helps keep the lithium ions in a stable state. Battery degradation could affect charging capacity. It should also be noted that some systems, like Windows, will actually shut down or hibernate before your battery hits 0%.

Sources indicate that if you find yourself flirting with that 0% a little more often than you'd like, it might be worth investigating whether there are reasons your battery is draining faster than normal. Most current laptops will last between 4 and 12 hours on a single charge, with some lasting even longer. This will vary depending on your laptop and what you're doing with it. For instance, gaming laptops won't last as long.

Otherwise, you could have apps running in the background that you don't need. Depending on the laptop you have, you might have some energy options to check out and tweak. Older software, higher temperatures or even plugged-in devices could all be contributing to your battery drain.

Recent findings suggest that in any case, it's worth keeping an eye on how much battery you have left if you're not connected to your charger. On the whole, draining your battery is mostly a self-inflicted annoyance. It's also not something you want to make a regular habit of doing, particularly if you're interested in making your battery last as long as possible.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

Industry observers note that we’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

Sources indicate that if you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro. It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

Sources indicate that if I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour, which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Industry observers note that hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

In a recent development, the Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere firm in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

Sources indicate that sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones….

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro. Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

According to recent reports, best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

In a recent development, for about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The organization recently introduced its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

In a recent development, I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone, Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands, Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5, the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.
  • Recent findings suggest that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon.
  • The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

Recent findings suggest that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified problem, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.

Sources indicate that the primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.

Industry observers note that this means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.

It has been revealed that in that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The firm has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

In a recent development, however, SpaceX still has a chance to make history on Saturday with the potential return of the Starship upper stage. SpaceX has never attempted to catch the vehicle’s upper stage.

Doing so will require Starship to pass a series of tests in orbit and subsequently during its return to Earth to ensure it is fully healthy. This is critical because Starship will be passing over parts of Mexico and the United States before returning to Starbase, and SpaceX does not want to endanger people on the ground. Additionally, it does not want to risk damage to its launch towers.

Industry observers note that if Starship passes these health checks, it would land at about 3:15 pm local time in Texas (21:15 UTC). If it does not, the company has earlier options to de-orbit the vehicle into an ocean.

It has been revealed that successfully returning Starship’s upper stage would be historic, as well as significant for SpaceX’s efforts to reuse the massive rocket. It would also give the organization valuable information about the vehicle’s performance during reentry.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest hurdles left in Starship’s development is the vehicle’s heat shield, which must protect the upper stage during its return through Earth’s atmosphere. More than that, SpaceX aims to make Starship rapidly reusable, and to do this, Starship’s tiles must be light and resilient.

SpaceX has been experimenting with tiles since the beginning of the Starship program, trying to find the right combination of low mass, heat resistance, and durability so the tiles require minimal refurbishment between launches. For this flight, SpaceX said it is applying learnings from the previous test flight in September, including additional retention mechanisms on tiles in areas deemed to be at the highest risk of falling off during ascent and addressing areas with a flow path for plasma to get behind the tiles.

Another problem on recent flights has been heat incursion into the small gaps between the edges of the tiles. According to SpaceX, this Starship has a large portion of the heat shield equipped with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles.

Tech Report: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An aging battery or a recent software enhancement could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.
  • Recent findings suggest that few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual.
  • According to recent reports, at the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An aging battery or a recent software enhancement could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.

Recent findings suggest that few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual. It gets to a point where it can no longer last a full day away from the charger. Under normal conditions, battery drain depends on what you're doing on your phone. Lighter uses like browsing the web and listening to music use less power, while taking lots of photos and playing games tend to drain your battery faster. But when your phone's battery suddenly drops without heavy use, something might be wrong.

According to recent reports, at the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying. Software can also cause your battery to drain faster, like when you install an iOS or Android patch, or when an app is constantly running in the background. If you've been noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster, here's what you can try to fix it.

Sources indicate that your phone doesn't know exactly how much charge is left in the battery. In fact, it estimates that number based on the battery's voltage and current, and sometimes that estimate is far off from reality. Eventually, the software recalculates it, and that's when you see the battery percentage suddenly drop by a significant amount instead of gradually. This happens more often with batteries in poor condition. As lithium-ion batteries age chemically, they no longer retain their full charge capacity and may also fail when the phone needs a power boost to perform a demanding task, like opening the camera or using GPS. As a result, your phone may think the battery is much lower than it actually is.

It has been revealed that smartphones have mechanisms to prevent this from happening. On iPhones, Apple has implemented a system that detects when the battery fails to reduce performance in order to avoid these spikes in power consumption. Temperature also has a major impact, as most phones are rated to operate at temperatures between 0° and 35° C (32° to 95° F). Using your phone at temperatures above that range can significantly reduce battery life. When your phone gets too hot, the battery will most likely drain much faster. It's best to stop using it until it returns to a normal temperature. Don't put it in a refrigerator, though, as the introduction of cold air can create condensation within the warmer phone.

Sources indicate that also, it's perfectly normal to see your phone's battery drain a little faster for a few hours or even days after an update. Both iOS and Android run a series of optimizations to put all the files in their proper places, and this increases battery consumption. The good news is that this is temporary, and everything goes back to normal once the indexing process is complete. A buggy app or a process constantly running in the background, especially if it uses your location, will also drain your phone's battery promptly.

Start by closing apps running in the background to see if your battery usage returns to normal. It's also worth taking a look at your privacy settings and limiting access to your location to only when you have an app open. This prevents your phone from constantly triggering the GPS. That alone should have a significant impact on reducing battery consumption. Also, check your phone's battery settings to see exactly which apps are draining your battery the most — both iOS and Android provide details on this.

Pixel 6 and later models have a Battery Diagnostics tool under Settings. On a Samsung Galaxy, open Settings, then Battery and tap View Details. For iPhone owners, it's as simple as going to Settings and opening the Battery menu. These menus usually include details about your phone's battery health. Apple, for example, says that the latest iPhones are designed to retain 80 percent of their original battery capacity through up to 1,000 charge cycles. If your phone's battery health is below 80 percent, you should probably replace it with a upcoming one — which, at least, is much cheaper than buying a new phone.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a latest audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio.
  • Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a fresh audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio.Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe claims the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release. The 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. A review of current vendor documentation turns up systems with higher published ceilings. Speechmatics' real-time transcription service says it can identify 50 speakers by default and up to 100 when the limit is increased, while Amazon Transcribe's diarization documentation specifies a maximum of 30 unique speakers, including for streaming transcription. (Speechmatics)Muse nevertheless lands toward the high end of the market, and Meta's broader proposition is arguably more notable than the raw maximum: high-capacity real-time diarization combined with low-latency transcription, endpointing, multilingual code-switching and aggressive API pricing in the same model.For enterprise developers building meeting systems, call analytics, live assistants or ambient AI, that combination could matter more than who holds the speaker-count record.Diarization is becoming part of the core voice stackTraditional speech recognition answers a relatively simple question: What was said? Diarization adds another: Who said it?That distinction becomes critical as transcripts feed downstream AI systems. A meeting assistant can correctly transcribe every sentence and still create an unreliable corporate record if it attributes an approval, commitment or objection to the wrong participant. The same matter affects customer-service analytics, compliance workflows and AI agents operating in rooms where several people can speak.Muse incorporates speaker attribution directly into its autoregressive multimodal architecture. Meta says audio arrives in 80-millisecond chunks, or 12.5 chunks per second, with each transformed into a soft token. At each step, the model decides whether to consume more audio or emit text. Meta calls this mechanism adaptive delay: rather than applying one latency budget to every word, Muse can wait longer when speech is ambiguous and commit earlier when it has enough context. Meta says reinforcement learning combines word-error-rate and delay rewards to train that behavior. Meta's technical explanation of Muse details the architecture. (Meta AI Research)Speaker attribution and endpointing then become part of the same token sequence. A <|start_of_turn|> token marks a potential new speaker turn, tokens such as <|speaker_A|> identify the speaker, and separate onset and endpoint tokens identify speech boundaries. Meta says it trains ASR, diarization and endpointing together rather than running speaker clustering as an unrelated downstream process.Meta's Model API speech-to-text documentation also exposes diarization as a first-class operating mode alongside push-to-talk and endpointing. Speaker labels such as A and B are scoped to a session rather than verified identities, and the API provides turn-level rather than word-level timestamps.20+ speakers is high, but Speechmatics goes considerably higherSpeaker-count comparisons require care because vendors implement diarization differently and do not all publish a maximum.Speechmatics currently makes the strongest explicit real-time capacity claim found in this review. Its real-time STT documentation says speaker diarization is available live, while its real-time FAQ says the system supports 50 speakers by default and can be increased to 100. AWS likewise exceeds Meta's stated figure: Amazon Transcribe can differentiate a maximum of 30 unique speakers, and AWS provides explicit instructions for speaker partitioning in a streaming transcription.Soniox supports diarization in both real-time and asynchronous processing, but documents a maximum of 15 speakers per session. AssemblyAI's streaming diarization system lets developers set max_speakers between one and 10. Both companies caution that live speaker attribution is more difficult because streaming systems must make decisions with less future audio context than offline models. xAI's current Speech-to-Text API also supports speaker diarization in streaming mode, but its documentation reviewed for this story does not publish a maximum diarized-speaker count, so a direct ceiling comparison with Muse is not possible. (X.ai Docs)That means it would be inaccurate to describe Muse's 20-plus capability as a new global record. The highest explicitly documented real-time number identified in this survey is Speechmatics' configurable 100-speaker ceiling.Meta also does not demonstrate 20-plus simultaneous participants in its launch material. Its principal live demonstration uses eight speakers, while its long-form recording contains 11 labeled participants. The 20-plus number is a stated model capability rather than the participant count in the public demos.At $0.18 per hour, Muse competes aggressively on priceMeta's pricing makes the competitive picture more interesting.According to its Muse Voice Transcribe developer page, Muse costs $3 per 1,000 minutes, or $0.18 per hour. Streaming and non-streaming transcription cost the same, and Meta says zero-data-retention processing is priced at parity with standard processing. Billing applies to audio actually processed and is rounded down to whole seconds.Standardizing publicly posted rates to one hour of streaming audio gives the following rough comparison:Streaming speech-to-text serviceApprox. public cost/hourReal-time diarizationSoniox stt-rt-v5$0.12Included; up to 15 speakersMeta Muse Voice Transcribe$0.18Included; 20+ speakersxAI Speech to Text$0.20Supported; maximum not statedSpeechmatics Real-time Standard$0.24Included; 50 default, configurable to 100Qwen3 ASR Flash Realtime~$0.324 internationalNo comparable maximum documented in source reviewedDeepgram Nova-3 Multilingual~$0.35 base / ~$0.47 with diarization$0.12/hour diarization add-onElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime$0.39 PAYGNot supported in real timeAssemblyAI Universal-3.5 Pro Realtime$0.45 base / $0.57 with diarization$0.12/hour add-on; up to 10 speakersGemini 3.5 Transcribe Live~$0.54 blendedNot supported in live modeAmazon Transcribe Streaming~$0.60 in AWS's N. Virginia streaming exampleIncluded; up to 30 speakersOpenAI GPT Live Transcribe$1.02Diarization not listed as a model capabilityThe comparison is necessarily imperfect. Qwen's price varies by deployment geography; its international real-time rate of $0.00009 per second works out to about $0.324 per hour. Google's Gemini figure is an estimated blended token cost rather than a flat hourly tariff. AWS prices vary by region and usage tier. Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a latest audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio.

Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe notes the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release.

In a recent development, the 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. A review of current vendor documentation turns up systems with higher published ceilings. Speechmatics' real-time transcription service notes it can identify 50 speakers by default and up to 100 when the limit is increased, while Amazon Transcribe's diarization documentation specifies a maximum of 30 unique speakers, including for streaming transcription. (Speechmatics).

Muse nevertheless lands toward the high end of the market, and Meta's broader proposition is arguably more crucial than the raw maximum: high-capacity real-time diarization combined with low-latency transcription, endpointing, multilingual code-switching and aggressive API pricing in the same model.

For enterprise developers building meeting systems, call analytics, live assistants or ambient AI, that combination could matter more than who holds the speaker-count record.

According to recent reports, traditional speech recognition answers a relatively simple question: What was remarked? Diarization adds another: Who said it?

That distinction becomes critical as transcripts feed downstream AI systems. A meeting assistant can correctly transcribe every sentence and still create an unreliable corporate record if it attributes an approval, commitment or objection to the wrong participant. The same concern affects customer-service analytics, compliance workflows and AI agents operating in rooms where several people can speak.

Muse incorporates speaker attribution directly into its autoregressive multimodal architecture. Meta states audio arrives in 80-millisecond chunks, or 12.5 chunks per second, with each transformed into a soft token. At each step, the model decides whether to consume more audio or emit text. Meta calls this mechanism adaptive delay: rather than applying one latency budget to every word, Muse can wait longer when speech is ambiguous and commit earlier when it has enough context. Meta says reinforcement learning combines word-error-rate and delay rewards to train that behavior. Meta's technical explanation of Muse details the architecture. (Meta AI Research).

Speaker attribution and endpointing then become part of the same token sequence. A <|start_of_turn|> token marks a potential new speaker turn, tokens such as <|speaker_A|> identify the speaker, and separate onset and endpoint tokens identify speech boundaries. Meta claims it trains ASR, diarization and endpointing together rather than running speaker clustering as an unrelated downstream process.

Meta's Model API speech-to-text documentation also exposes diarization as a first-class operating mode alongside push-to-talk and endpointing. Speaker labels such as A and B are scoped to a session rather than verified identities, and the API provides turn-level rather than word-level timestamps.

Speaker-count comparisons require care because vendors implement diarization differently and do not all publish a maximum.

Speechmatics currently makes the strongest explicit real-time capacity claim found in this review. Its real-time STT documentation says speaker diarization is available live, while its real-time FAQ says the system supports 50 speakers by default and can be increased to 100.

AWS likewise exceeds Meta's stated figure: Amazon Transcribe can differentiate a maximum of 30 unique speakers, and AWS provides explicit instructions for speaker partitioning in a streaming transcription.

In a recent development, soniox supports diarization in both real-time and asynchronous processing, but documents a maximum of 15 speakers per session. AssemblyAI's streaming diarization system lets developers set max_speakers between one and 10. Both companies caution that live speaker attribution is more difficult because streaming systems must make decisions with less future audio context than offline models.

Recent findings suggest that xAI's current Speech-to-Text API also supports speaker diarization in streaming mode, but its documentation reviewed for this story does not publish a maximum diarized-speaker count, so a direct ceiling comparison with Muse is not possible. (X.ai Docs).

Industry observers note that that means it would be inaccurate to describe Muse's 20-plus capability as a fresh global record. The highest explicitly documented real-time number identified in this survey is Speechmatics' configurable 100-speaker ceiling.

Meta also does not demonstrate 20-plus simultaneous participants in its launch material. Its principal live demonstration uses eight speakers, while its long-form recording contains 11 labeled participants. The 20-plus number is a stated model capability rather than the participant count in the public demos.

Meta's pricing makes the competitive picture more interesting.

In a recent development, according to its Muse Voice Transcribe developer page, Muse costs $3 per 1,000 minutes, or $0.18 per hour. Streaming and non-streaming transcription cost the same, and Meta claims zero-data-retention processing is priced at parity with standard processing. Billing applies to audio actually processed and is rounded down to whole seconds.

Standardizing publicly posted rates to one hour of streaming audio gives the following rough comparison:.

Industry observers note that the comparison is necessarily imperfect. Qwen's price varies by deployment geography; its international real-time rate of $0.00009 per second works out to about $0.324 per hour. Google's Gemini figure is an estimated blended token cost rather than a flat hourly tariff. AWS prices vary by region and usage tier. ElevenLabs lists $0.39 per hour on its API pricing page but advertises $0.28 per hour or lower on annual Business looks.

It has been revealed that deepgram's pricing particularly illustrates why feature-level comparisons matter: its current Nova-3 Multilingual streaming rate is about $0.35 per hour, but speaker diarization costs another $0.002 per minute, bringing the comparable total to roughly $0.47 per hour. AssemblyAI similarly lists $0.45 per hour for Universal-3.5 Pro Realtime and another $0.12 per hour for streaming diarization.

Cartesia is harder to normalize because Ink-2 is packaged through monthly credit plans rather than a simple metered PAYG hourly rate. Its $5 Pro strategy includes roughly nine hours and 16 minutes of Ink-2 transcription, which works out to about $0.54 per transcription hour if every credit is consumed exclusively on STT. That should not be treated as equivalent to a standalone $0.54 hourly API tariff.

Sources indicate that even with those caveats, Muse's positioning is clear. It is not the absolute cheapest streaming transcription service — Soniox presently publishes a lower equivalent rate — but $0.18 per hour with diarization included puts Meta toward the low end of the market, especially against providers that charge separately for speaker attribution.

At 1,000 hours of processed audio, Meta's public rate implies roughly $180 in transcription charges.

Price matters less if it comes with a large accuracy penalty. Meta's benchmark material argues the opposite.

On the Artificial Analysis AA-WER Streaming Index supplied with the launch, Muse records a 3.1% final-transcription word error rate, ahead of Cartesia Ink-2 at 3.4%, ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime at 3.6%, Qwen3 ASR Flash Realtime at 3.7%, GPT Live Transcribe and Grok Speech to Text Streaming at 3.9%, and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and AssemblyAI U3.5 Realtime Pro at 4.0%.

Meta points out that Muse took the number one spot on third-party independent AI benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis' streaming speech-to-text evaluation as of September 1. Meta published the following benchmark charts in its launch post.

In a recent development, its diarization result may be even more relevant to the product's positioning. Meta reports an average 17.5% diarization error rate across AMI-IHM, AMI-SDM and VoxConverse, lower than the competing systems shown in its chart.

Speaker capacity and diarization error rate should not be conflated. A platform capable of representing 100 people is not automatically better at correctly attributing speech than one supporting 20, and Meta's benchmark does not test every competitor operating at its advertised maximum speaker count.

It has been revealed that there are deployment tradeoffs as well. Meta's API at the moment provides turn-level but not word-level timestamps, and it does not expose word-level confidence scores, sound-event detection or emotion detection. The documentation also specifies eight concurrent streams per tenant by default and real-time sessions of up to 60 minutes before an application must reconnect.

Still, Muse's launch creates an unusually sharp price-performance proposition. Its 20-plus-speaker diarization does not establish a world record, but the record may be the less important metric. For enterprise developers, the larger question is whether a service can preserve speaker attribution, accurate text and usable turn boundaries while a complicated real-world conversation is still unfolding.

At $0.18 per hour, with 20-plus-speaker diarization inside the same real-time model that currently leads Meta's supplied streaming accuracy benchmarks, Muse Voice Transcribe gives enterprise teams a serious latest option for meeting intelligence, live transcription and voice-agent infrastructure — while putting additional pressure on competitors to compete on speaker-aware accuracy and total operating cost, not merely raw speech recognition.

#54. This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)

This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected.
  • That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects.
  • In a recent development, you might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

In a recent development, you might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.

Kim notes everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.

Giving AI a physical body isn't fresh, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.

OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.

The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.

Recent findings suggest that it can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim notes, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.

The catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.

Recent findings suggest that kim notes she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.

The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.

But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.

According to recent reports, it's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic announced a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.

Kim says that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.

“Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim says. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this.".

After spending a few weeks with it and traveling across the Atlantic, here is what you should know about the Kuxiu K4 Air.

Sources indicate that so if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your substantial three Apple products, and looks fantastic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he stated the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

I spoke to Leo Wang, the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle manufacturer Pony.ai, this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Recent findings suggest that demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

Industry observers note that “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”.

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang mentioned Chinese companies have already been preparing.

It has been revealed that “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he stated. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”.

It has been revealed that may Mobility looks to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company mentioned it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.).

Newmo, a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI.

ParkBee, a Dutch parking technology firm, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations.

Port, an urban logistics organization, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord.

Sources indicate that lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency mentioned that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software revision intended to fix the problem. Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its latest HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

According to recent reports, the UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

At the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

According to recent reports, UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

Meanwhile, the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro is a pan-tilt-zoom camera meant to be used inside to capture events in an entire room. It features 4K imaging, 360-degree pan and 160-degree vertical tilt while supporting up to 8x digital zoom, motion tracking, and even baby-cry detection. It also has a physical shutter for your privacy.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

Industry observers note that you can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.

#49. 10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1858 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.
  • Industry observers note that for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live.
  • It has been revealed that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.

Industry observers note that for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live. If you've only used it for basic text, you've probably missed how Apple has added new features to the mix that can solve complex equations, draw graphs, transcribe audio and turn your doodles into images. iOS 27 brought even more, including smarter Siri integration and divider lines, so the app is more capable than ever.

It has been revealed that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended. On the iPhone, that means the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and any iPhone 16 model or later. Those features are flagged along the way, along with anything that requires a specific version of iOS.

The Notes app has a calculator hiding inside it, with the math happening while you're typing. Since iOS 18, when you type an equation and add an equals sign, Math Notes fills in the answer on the spot. It also works with variables, so if you write "dinner = $42" and change that value later, every result that uses it updates automatically. That makes it a surprisingly easy way to split the bill or plan a monthly budget.

Math Notes can do more than give you simple answers. After you type an equation that starts with "y =", tap the equals sign and choose Insert Graph to plot what you've typed right inside the note. If you change the variable, the graph changes automatically to match. It's a neat tool for students to check their homework without a dedicated graphing app.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have a physical scanner at home, there's no need to download a dedicated scanner app to replace it. Tapping the attachment button in any note reveals the Scan Documents option, where Notes will capture a page automatically, including cropping and straightening it for you. The scanner also offers a flash option and image filters if needed.

In Auto mode, you don't even need to tap on the shutter button; the system captures the document once it detects the page's edges and you're holding your iPhone steady. You can scan multiple pages into a single document, which is useful for contracts, lease agreements or anything else that runs longer than a page.

In a recent development, if the document needs a signature, open the scan, tap Markup, then go to Add > Signature. Use a saved signature or draw a upcoming one with your finger, then resize it and drag it into place. It's an easy way to sign and send a form without taking a printout of the pages. Scans are saved to the note as PDFs, which you can annotate.

In a recent development, notes can double as a recorder: choose Record Audio in any note to record and transcribe everything your phone hears. The transcript is searchable, so you can jump into the relevant part of a long lecture instead of scrubbing through the entire session. On iPhone models with Apple Intelligence, Notes can summarize entire recorded lectures or meetings. Phone calls you record also land in Notes inside the Call Recordings folder with a transcript.

In a recent development, the iPhone already has a dedicated recording app in Voice Memos, so it's worth knowing when to use which. Notes is the better pick when the recording is part of something bigger. For a class or a meeting, for example, you can type your own notes, add photos of the whiteboard and keep the recording all in the same note. Everything stays together, so you won't have to switch between multiple apps when you're going through your notes at home. Meanwhile, Voice Memos makes more sense when the audio itself matters most, like an interview you blueprint to edit or share.

According to recent reports, if you need some help when drawing, sketch something rough with the Markup tools, then pick Image Wand from the same tool palette and circle your sketch. Add a few words describing the image you want, and Apple Intelligence will turn your doodle into a polished image.

In a recent development, you also have the option to circle an empty spot in the note and create a latest image based on the text around it. Afterward, fine-tune the image by adding or removing descriptive words. If your note is a packing list for a beach trip, for instance, it will generate a matching seaside illustration to sit at the top.

In iOS 27, Image Playground, which powers this feature in the Notes app, got a newly introduced model that can make photorealistic images, not just stylized ones. Since iOS 27.2, most images you generate or edit carry a SynthID watermark, which the SynthID detection website uses to know something was made by AI.

In a recent development, your notes don't have to be only for you; it's possible to share a specific note or an entire folder with your family, friends and coworkers, then everyone can make changes in real time. This is ideal for a household grocery list or a group blueprint for a trip. The person who creates the shared note remains in control of who can do what.

Just tap the Share button in the note you want to add people to, then choose whether each person can make changes or only view it. Type @ followed by someone's name and they'll get a notification pointing them to the note. If several people are editing the same note, the activity view and highlights show who changed what and when. And in iOS 27, the Shared folder now sits at the top of the folders list with a newly introduced icon, so multi-person notes are easier to spot.

Sources indicate that the Notes app can help with the actual writing you do. Select some text, tap the Apple Intelligence button in the toolbar and pick an option from the Writing Tools menu. This can proofread your text for spelling and grammar mistakes and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional or more concise tone.

The suite is also useful for reshaping messy notes. It's able to create a summary of a long note or pull out its key points, which is handy after a meeting or before an exam. It will also turn a block of text into a bulleted list or even convert it into a table. If you've jotted down a few phone looks with their prices and data limits, for example, the Table option can organize them into neat rows and columns so they're easier to compare.

Writing Tools isn't limited to just the Notes app; it works almost anywhere you can type on the iPhone, including third-party apps. In iOS 27, Apple Intelligence also suggests ways to improve your writing.

Industry observers note that long notes quickly become messy and hard to organize, but Notes has a few tools to keep them neat. With iOS 18 and newer, you have the option to collapse any heading to minimize sections you're not working on. This means the final version is a bit cleaner to view, while it's also easier to manage everything while writing.

Recent findings suggest that if that's not enough, you can also highlight text in different colors, curating them by sections, information or any other preference. To do so, select the text, tap the Aa format button and pick a color. Notes offers five color options to choose from: pink, purple, orange, mint and blue. iOS 27 also added divider lines, which gives another option to tidy up a mess. Place your cursor where you want a break, open the edit menu and choose Insert Divider Line. If someone views the note on iOS 26 or prior, the divider lines show up as three hyphens(—), so nothing breaks.

iOS 27 also added section links to the mix, letting you link to a specific section of a note where tapping the link jumps straight there. That's particularly useful for a table of contents in a long note. Pasting Markdown now converts it to formatted text automatically, and a new Copy as Markdown option easily brings notes to other apps with the formatting intact.

Sources indicate that iOS 26 added a reed pen to the Markup tools, which is designed for a traditional calligraphy experience. Like the actual writing instrument, your strokes get thicker or thinner depending on the direction you draw in. It's a unique way to write, especially for special occasions like birthdays and invitations. You'll find the reed pen in the list of Markup tools; tapping it again after selecting it is how you pick a preset.

It has been revealed that there are five angle presets to choose from, with the one you pick deciding which stroke direction gives the thickest line. The angle is fixed no matter how you hold your finger, so your strokes stay consistent. Apart from the Notes app, the reed pen also works in Freeform, Journal and Preview — basically anywhere the Markup tools are available.

Recent findings suggest that the search bar in the Notes app is smarter than it looks and than how most people casually use it. Beyond your own typed notes, it can search handwriting, objects in images and text in scanned documents. Tap the search button, then type a word from a page or a photo. If you scanned a receipt months ago, searching for the store's name should bring it up. It's an easy way to find snippets from longer notes, especially when you're transcribing lectures or meetings.

According to recent reports, this turns your Notes library into a practical place to store paperwork you might need in the future. Consider storing information like warranty cards, appliance manuals, prescriptions and receipts all in Notes, then you can find them by searching for a word on the page instead of scrolling through dozens of scans and navigating file names.

Industry observers note that siri and Notes finally work together properly in iOS 27. Siri can create notes with generated content, like information it pulled from the web, instead of only typing what you say. Ask it to put together a packing list for a trip and save it to a new note, and it will comply. This really comes in handy for smaller notes or basic reminders, as well as capturing ideas on the spot when you can't stop to type.

It can also add to an existing note or clean up a list before saving it. If you've got a messy, unformatted list, ask Siri to tidy it up and add it to the right note. Of course, the full power of this requires Siri AI, which introduced in English first. iOS 27.2 added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish. Older iPhone models can also create notes with Siri, but without the AI-generated content, which slightly limits the feature. But the basics are still there to jot down ideas.

#48. Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash is built for agents, while its Cyber twin hunts vulnerabilities

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2167 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Venturebeat ↗ Open Full Page

Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash is built for agents, while its Cyber twin hunts vulnerabilities

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Venturebeat

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that google keeps cranking out Flash models: the company on Wednesday revealed two versions of a new 3.8 Flash.
  • Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the manufacturer on Wednesday unveiled two versions of a upcoming 3.8 Flash.
  • The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google keeps cranking out Flash models: the company on Wednesday revealed two versions of a new 3.8 Flash. The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation.Google CEO Sundar Pichai said in an X post that 3.8 Flash delivers “significant leaps” from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning. For instance, it outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark, at far lower cost. Meanwhile, Flash Cyber is the company’s “most capable” cybersecurity model, Pichai said; it also matches frontier-level performance when it comes to discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale. The model achieved 86.2% on the CyberGym cybersecurity benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench, which evaluates AI patching abilities. In an internal Google benchmark, the model achieved a more than 70% success rate discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages, Pichai said. 3.8 is Google’s third Flash release in six weeks and comes quickly on the heels of version 3.7. 3.8 working "harder" with "greater diligence"3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise; devs can try it out in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, Android Studio, or generate UIs in Stitch. It is priced at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — the same introductory pricing as Gemini 3.7 Flash — and people can customize and adjust model effort levels based on their needs around quality, cost, and latency. For instance, when compute efficiency is a priority, they can adjust to lower token overhead, or simply continue working with 3.7 Flash, which is “fully supported for efficiency-first workloads,” Google senior product director Tulsee Doshi and Gemini security lead Raluca Ada Popa wrote in a blog post. “3.8 Flash works harder,” exhibiting “greater diligence” with complex tasks like executing extra reasoning steps, although at times it may use more tokens to maximize performance, Doshi and Popa note. The model has a 1M-token input window and a 64K-token output limit, and can ingest text as well as images, audio, video, and PDF files. 3.8 Flash was evaluated across numerous benchmarks testing coding, multimodal capabilities, computer use, long-context and knowledge work, and scientific reasoning. Google indicates it also does well in specialized knowledge domains requiring more in-depth analysis and reporting. For instance, the model outperformed its predecessor and other frontier models on benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 for finance, and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for law; it also scored 54.9% on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)-Verified, reflecting its ability to take on multi-step reasoning tasks across subjects like math, science, and humanities. In one example shared by Google, Gemini 3.8 Flash built a game with a simple prompt using looping techniques in Google’s Antigravity platform. The game uses puzzles, storytelling that changes based on the environment, and images and textures from Nano Banana to create a 3D experience (in this case a wizard navigating a castle). In other instances, the model created a fully-functional DOS version of Google Maps featuring interactive locations, directions, and street views; a 3D visualizer that automatically decomposed devices into layers for inspection with a slider capability; and a topographic map of famous geographical sites based on real datasets from the U.S. Geological Survey, complete with real-time cross-sections, 2D projections, and scientific explanations. According to Arena.ai, 3.8 Flash landed at No. 14 in Agent Arena, ranking above DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and showed a significant jump over Gemini 3.7 Flash (which sits all the way down at No. 32). It debuted at No. 7 in Text Arena, ahead of Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash. It improved over 3.7 Flash in several areas: multi-turn requests, writing, literature, and language, longer queries, hard prompts, coding, instruction following, software and IT services, and business, management and financial ops. Flash Cyber is already securing Google's codeFlash Cyber is initially being rolled out to “trusted defenders” through Google’s Fairwind Program, which prioritizes government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and other partners looking for advanced cyber defense capabilities. Organizations can apply for access. Google says the model version has undergone “rigorous training” in the cybersecurity domain and represents a “significant leap in prompt injection robustness.” It is particularly adept at autonomous vulnerability discovery — at least, based on internal Gemini benchmarks — and automated patching. It is also very good at coding, Popa said in a video. The goal was to equip defenders with expert-level capabilities to give them a leg up over threat actors (whether malicious, fellow AI agents, or human hackers). “We have invested in vulnerability fixing from the start, and prioritized it over offensive capabilities like exploitation,” Doshi and Popa explain. The model ships a more permissive set of mitigations for cybersecurity safeguards — which is why, for now, it is only being shared with limited partners — and safeguards against misuse in cyber offense and areas like chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN).Google is already using 3.8 Flash Cyber to secure its own code; it produced 2.6 times more correct patches in Chrome vulnerabilities versus much larger commercial models. Wiz — which Google acquired earlier this year at a historic $32 billion — reported that 3.8 Flash Cyber had 7.5% to 9.7% higher recall of real-world vulnerabilities on an internal penetration testing benchmark at 2.3 to 5.2 times lower cost than leading frontier models. Similarly, Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research found a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours with 3.8 Flash Cyber. Typically, that research and discovery would take months, Google claims. AI agents are “incredibly skilled” at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Popa said. Scanning large codebases with significant AI models is expensive, and defenders are overwhelmed. “In cybersecurity, attackers need only find one significant flaw over millions of lines of code. Defenders have to remove every one of those flaws to be able to defend against attackers.” Doug Turner, engineering director for Chrome, described a “vulnerability apocalypse” in recent months due to generative AI. “Simply overnight, we saw a hockey stick increase in the number of software vulnerabilities reported through our vulnerability research program,” he said in a video. One interesting vulnerability 3.8 Flash Cyber discovered had been in Chromium and Chrome for 13 years, he explained. It was a “very subtle bug” that dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers looked at but never flagged. “Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is going to allow us to create better suggested fixes so that developers’ lives can get a lot easier.”.

Industry observers note that flash Cyber is initially being rolled out to “trusted defenders” through Google’s Fairwind Program, which prioritizes government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and other partners looking for advanced cyber defense capabilities. Organizations can apply for access.

Google says the model version has undergone “rigorous training” in the cybersecurity domain and represents a “significant leap in prompt injection robustness.” It is particularly adept at autonomous vulnerability discovery — at least, based on internal Gemini benchmarks — and automated patching. It is also very good at coding, Popa said in a video.

The goal was to equip defenders with expert-level capabilities to give them a leg up over threat actors (whether malicious, fellow AI agents, or human hackers). “We have invested in vulnerability fixing from the start, and prioritized it over offensive capabilities like exploitation,” Doshi and Popa explain.

The model ships a more permissive set of mitigations for cybersecurity safeguards — which is why, for now, it is only being shared with limited partners — and safeguards against misuse in cyber offense and areas like chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN).

Google is already using 3.8 Flash Cyber to secure its own code; it produced 2.6 times more correct patches in Chrome vulnerabilities versus much larger commercial models.

Wiz — which Google acquired earlier this year at a historic $32 billion — reported that 3.8 Flash Cyber had 7.5% to 9.7% higher recall of real-world vulnerabilities on an internal penetration testing benchmark at 2.3 to 5.2 times lower cost than leading frontier models. Similarly, Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research found a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours with 3.8 Flash Cyber. Typically, that research and discovery would take months, Google claims.

According to recent reports, AI agents are “incredibly skilled” at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Popa said. Scanning large codebases with big AI models is expensive, and defenders are overwhelmed. “In cybersecurity, attackers need only find one significant flaw over millions of lines of code. Defenders have to remove every one of those flaws to be able to defend against attackers.”.

Doug Turner, engineering director for Chrome, described a “vulnerability apocalypse” in recent months due to generative AI. “Simply overnight, we saw a hockey stick increase in the number of software vulnerabilities reported through our vulnerability research program,” he stated in a video.

One interesting vulnerability 3.8 Flash Cyber discovered had been in Chromium and Chrome for 13 years, he explained. It was a “very subtle bug” that dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers looked at but never flagged. “Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is going to allow us to create better suggested fixes so that developers’ lives can get a lot easier.”.

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already mentioned that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

In a recent development, U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.

"Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Manufacturer," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.

Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.

The tech giant, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.

Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation.".

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.

The firm added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.

— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.
